name: Mad honey

lead: Mad honey is honey made by bees foraging on Rhododendron flowers, containing grayanotoxins. It is produced mainly in the Black Sea region of Turkey (where it is called deli bal) and in the Himalayas of Nepal, and it has been used as a folk remedy for centuries.

People take it as a tonic and as an aphrodisiac, and in appearance-oriented communities it is discussed as a vitality or libido booster. The link to looks is indirect and claimed: better energy and drive. Research on mad honey is mostly case reports of poisoning rather than trials of benefit.

paras: Traditionally a small amount is eaten on its own or stirred into milk or a drink, and it is sold online as a specialty honey. Potency varies by season, altitude and hive, which is why intoxication is dose-dependent and unpredictable.

Grayanotoxins keep sodium channels open and can cause dizziness, nausea, low blood pressure, slow heart rate and heart block. A review of 1,199 cases found no deaths, with most patients treated with atropine and fluids and discharged within a day. Most cases involve middle-aged men, and some countries have restricted its sale.

angle.text: People take mad honey as a traditional tonic and aphrodisiac. Any benefit to looks would come from claimed vitality rather than a change in the face or body. Research documents poisoning effects rather than benefits.

lead: Mad honey is honey contaminated by grayanotoxins from Rhododendron nectar and pollen. It is dark, slightly bitter and produced mainly in Turkey's Black Sea mountains and the Himalayas of Nepal.[1][2]

It has long been used in folk medicine: as an aphrodisiac, for high blood pressure and for stomach complaints.[3][4] In online circles it is discussed as a vitality and libido tonic, which supports energy, confidence and the general sense of a healthy, vigorous presence; the effect on appearance is not direct.
Published research is dominated by case reports and reviews of poisoning. A systematic review of 1,199 cases from 1981 to 2014 reported no deaths.[5]

paras: Mad honey is produced when bees visit Rhododendron flowers; in Turkey the main species are R. luteum and R. ponticum, and in Nepal the Himalayan giant honey bee builds cliff nests harvested by Gurung honey hunters.[1] Potency varies with season, elevation and weather, and honey from a single hive is more concentrated than blended commercial honey.[1]

Xenophon's Anabasis describes Greek soldiers near Trabzon in 401 BCE becoming disoriented and sick after eating it, recovering in a day or two.[1][2] Classical writers considered it a treatment for madness, and in 65 BCE King Mithridates is said to have left combs of it for pursuing Roman soldiers.[1] In the eighteenth century about 25 tons a year are reported to have been exported to Europe to add to alcoholic drinks, and a German scientist isolated andromedotoxin from Trabzon honey in 1891.[1]
In Turkey a spoonful is sometimes taken in milk as a tonic, and users believe it helps sexual performance; it is also used for hypertension, ulcers and gastritis.[1][3][4]

No trials of benefit have been published. Research consists of case series and reviews. A systematic review of 1,199 poisoning cases found most patients were men aged 41 to 65, with sinus bradycardia in about 80 percent and complete atrioventricular block in about 46 percent; most were treated with atropine and saline and discharged within 24 hours.[5]

Grayanotoxins act on sodium channels and muscarinic receptors, causing hypotension, slow heart rate and rhythm disorders, with dizziness, vomiting, sweating and paraesthesia.[3][4] Mild cases need only observation, while severe ones can need intravenous treatment.[2] A 2023 EFSA assessment classed grayanotoxins as genotoxic in vivo and could not assess chronic risk, and South Korea banned the honey in 2005.[1]
A 2026 Hacker News thread discussed mad honey being sold online and the risk of heart effects.[6]
